title: Phage bet-hedging via 10,000-fold reversion, and first humanized EBV antibodies
dek: Phages use SSR-driven 10,000-fold reversion for bet-hedging; humanized EBV antibodies block tumors in vivo; vaccines advance on multiple fronts.
why: From phage evolution to EBV antibodies to cognitive laziness, one thread links molecular mechanisms, drug development, and science communication. The antibody data in the latter half is especially hardcore.
who: Researchers working on phages or antibodies, investors tracking EBV vaccine progress, and engineers who want to understand the predicament of science communication.
skip: The first half hour of phage details is fairly basic; if you only care about antibody development, start at 50:44.

points.h: Phages deliberately break a fraction of their offspring
points.body: Jolene introduces a Nature Microbiology paper: homopolymeric nucleotide repeats (SSRs) in phage genes are prone to slippage during replication, causing insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame. This means a subset of progeny always fails to make functional proteins. This randomness is the basis of bet-hedging: most sequences fit the current environment, but a persistent low-level variant can become the survivor if the environment shifts abruptly. The population buys long-term survival at a small cost.

points.h: No need to pre-adapt: reversion is 10,000 times faster
points.body: The paper measured reversion frequencies at SSR regions, finding them about 10,000 times higher than typical point mutations. This magnitude means phages can rapidly switch a gene's function on or off within very few generations, rather than waiting for rare point mutations. Jolene stresses that this mechanism lets the population respond to environmental change without pre-adaptation—it simply generates diversity continuously and waits for selection.

points.h: T7 has zero SSRs; bet-hedging is not standard
points.body: In the Basel phage collection, T7's genome has no SSRs. Rich comments that T7 is 'businesslike'—straightforward, without these fancy mechanisms. This contrast shows that SSRs are not a universal feature of phages but an evolutionary strategy in certain lineages occupying specific niches. Even lytic phages infecting the same host can be organized very differently at the genomic level.

points.h: Humanization is hard not in the variable region but the constant region
points.body: When converting a mouse antibody into a humanized one, there is a conflict between the variable and constant regions; someone must spend years adjusting the constant region to be compatible with the variable region to produce a therapeutic antibody. Brienne says this was her 'aha' moment—she had not understood why mouse antibodies were necessary. Vincent adds that directly using human antibodies may not yield the desired antibody; the mouse platform's advantage is the ability to screen many clones and engineer the antigen, obtaining a full B-cell clonal diversification process, after which classic hybridoma technology is still needed to get monoclonal antibodies.

points.h: Hybridoma screening ends with only 10 antibodies
points.body: The group immunized mice with recombinant GP350 and GP42, generated hybridomas, plated them in 384-well plates, and used antigen-coupled magnetic beads for high-throughput flow cytometry screening, testing both binding and infection inhibition. Positive clones were subcloned and their heavy/light chain genes sequenced, then expressed as recombinant human IgG1 antibodies. The final result: 2 GP350-binding antibodies and 8 GP42-neutralizing antibodies. The whole pipeline shows the complete path from animal immunization to recombinant antibodies.

points.h: Antibodies also block EBV challenge in vivo
points.body: In two types of immunodeficient mice engrafted with human CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells, 500 micrograms of antibody (ATX42-2, ATX350-2, MO1, etc.) was injected intraperitoneally, followed by intravenous EBV challenge, with observation for 11 weeks. Results showed these antibodies prevented tumor formation, suppressed viral DNA replication, and blocked splenomegaly. Spleens from ATX42-2- and MO1-treated mice had no detectable EBER-positive cells. This means human antibodies protect against EBV challenge in vivo, not just neutralize in vitro.

points.h: Alum-adjuvanted subunit is dead; nanoparticle vaccines live
points.body: A GP350 subunit vaccine with alum adjuvant failed to induce protective immunity in trials; GP42 is conformationally variable, making it hard to elicit the right antibodies. But a GP350 ferritin nanoparticle vaccine has shown safety and immunogenicity in phase I, with seropositive participants remaining EBV-free up to 540 days. Also in development are a GH/GP42 ferritin nanoparticle and Moderna's mRNA vaccine (containing four antigens). Vincent expresses disappointment that the paper did not test combinations of GP350 and GP42 antibodies.

points.h: Anti-vaxxers may lack not information but the will to think
points.body: Vincent revisits 'Thinking, Fast and Slow,' quoting Joshua Reynolds: 'There is no expedient to which a man will not resort to avoid the real labor of thinking.' He argues that cognitive economy may partly explain anti-science and anti-vaccine attitudes: deep thinking is costly, and people prefer the effortless System 1 thinking. He then says, 'That's laziness—cognitive laziness.' This view attributes the science communication predicament to humans' default cognitive mode rather than a simple lack of information.
